output.title: Designing against eval drift starts with a threshold
output.body:
If you are automating a recurring workflow, eval drift is not a theory problem. It is the question of how you will know the system is no longer matching the work it was built to handle. In a small business, that often shows up in customer replies, invoices, or lead handling. The AI may look fine on the sample you used to build it, then real messages, edge cases, or a process change start pulling it off course.

The practical move is to define the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate. For example, if an assistant is classifying inbox messages, decide what “correct enough” means and what level of manual review means the system needs a reset. That threshold is a control, not a promise.

For owner-operators, the boundary stays human. If the workflow touches money movement or any other high-risk decision, the machine should not decide on its own. Build for alerts, review, and a clear handoff back to you when confidence drops or patterns change. That is design intent, not a claim that the system already does it.

The next step is simple: write one sentence for the workflow, such as, “If X changes, we pause automation and review Y.” Then ask two questions: how would I know it is drifting, and what decision do I want to keep?】【。
